clue.text: Thus with passion I cry out, all excited about it?

definitions.text: Thus with passion I cry out, all excited about it?

parts.note: a wax is an old word for a fit of temper or passion

indicators.note: excited letters are stirred up, so these are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone describes how they shout out in a fervour of enthusiasm.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'wax' is an old phrase for growing heated, and the whole clue paints a gushing speaker; 'excited' signals the anagram of I CRY ALL.
explanation.definitionFit: To wax lyrical is to talk with great enthusiasm, the exclaiming fervour the whole clue paints.

clue.text: Frolicsome, see, going without sleep

indicators.note: going without here means going outside, so one word wraps round the other

parts.note: to spy is to see or catch sight of
kip is British slang for a sleep or nap

explanation.surface: A playful person is seen to be going without any rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going without' reads as lacking, but here it means placed outside the other piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Skippy describes someone light-footed and playful, inclined to skip about.

clue.text: Inherent sex appeal enthralling one chap amongst others

indicators.note: enthralling means holding captive, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: IT is a long-standing slang term for sex appeal

indicators.note: amongst means placed in the middle of the other piece

parts.note: other chaps, that is, men
a single chap is a man

explanation.surface: A man with natural allure stands out from his fellows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'amongst' and 'enthralling' both signal containment, one nested inside the other; IT for sex appeal is an old convention.
explanation.definitionFit: Immanent means existing within or inherent, a synonym in philosophical use.

clue.text: Hail performance involving company stand-in's debut

indicators.note: involving means wrapping round, so one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: a performance on stage is an act

indicators.note: a debut is a first appearance, so only the opening letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: An understudy gets a debut in a company show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hail' looks like weather but is the verb to call out to someone; 'involving' and 'debut' work as noted.
explanation.definitionFit: To hail someone is to call out to them, and to accost is to approach and address a stranger boldly.

clue.text: Gee! Boy I love left one bunch of flowers

parts.note: gee is the spoken name of the letter G
a boy is a lad
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: An excited lad exclaims as he leaves a single bouquet behind.
explanation.definitionFit: Gladioli are tall spiky flowers usually sold in stems, plural of gladiolus.

clue.text: Stink about one's taking in lodger

indicators.note: taking in means admitting inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: PG stands for paying guest, a lodger
on means concerning or about

explanation.surface: Someone complains that a lodger has brought a smell into the house.
explanation.walkthrough: PG, for paying guest, is the British term for a lodger; 'taking in' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Pong is British slang for a bad smell.

clue.text: Go to pieces without first being shown instrument of torture

indicators.note: without first means the opening letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: to crack is to break down under pressure, to go to pieces

explanation.surface: A prisoner breaks down once shown the torture device.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without first' drops C from CRACK.
explanation.definitionFit: The rack was a frame used to stretch victims, a classic torture device.

clue.text: Air-filled container?

parts.note: air is read as a tune rather than the atmosphere, so this is a box that holds melodies

explanation.surface: A box full of nothing but air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Air' means a tune here: the box plays melodies when opened.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical box plays a tune, and a tune is called an air.

clue.text: Get a month ahead by covert means?

definitions.text: Get a month ahead by covert means?

parts.words: Get a month ahead by covert means?
parts.note: read literally, a calendar month is stolen to get ahead; the idiom means to gain an early advantage

explanation.surface: Someone sneakily skips ahead in the calendar.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is taken literally: steal = covert means, and the third month of the year is the month taken.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to gain an advantage over a rival by acting first, read here as taking a calendar month.

clue.text: Book covering court action after error

indicators.note: after places the court piece behind the error piece

parts.note: a slip is a small mistake
a case is a lawsuit heard in court

explanation.surface: A legal case follows a clerical blunder.
explanation.definitionFit: A slipcase is a protective box into which a book slides.

clue.text: I returned to nurse ailing lad in closing stage of life

indicators.note: to nurse is to hold close, so the other piece sits inside
returned means sent back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: ego is Latin for I, the self

indicators.note: ailing means unwell, so the letters are disordered

explanation.surface: A carer comes back to look after a sick young man near the end of his life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned', 'ailing' and 'to nurse' each work on a piece: a backward Latin I holds the scrambled lad.
explanation.definitionFit: Being elderly is the final phase of a lifespan.

clue.text: Breaking of white horses here? No grey, oddly

indicators.note: oddly suggests the letters are set out in a strange order

explanation.surface: Wild horses are broken, but not the grey one, oddly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'White horses' are waves with foam crests, not animals; a groyne is where they break. 'oddly' rearranges NO GREY.
explanation.definitionFit: A groyne is a sea barrier built out from the shore that waves crash against.

clue.text: Description of coast in letters read out

indicators.note: read out means spoken, so the word is judged by how it sounds

parts.note: literal means relating to letters of the alphabet

explanation.surface: Coastal scenery is described in letters read aloud.
explanation.walkthrough: LITERAL, said aloud, sounds like the shoreline adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Littoral means relating to the shore, so it describes a coastal zone.

clue.text: Explosion of lethal fury catching everyone's attention?

indicators.note: an explosion blows things apart, so the letters fly into a new order

parts.note: rage is fury

explanation.surface: A lethal outburst of anger gets noticed by all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Explosion of' signals the anagram of LETHAL; the definition is a question because a fad catches attention without being defined by it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something hugely fashionable draws everyone's interest.

clue.text: Tries to win many a trial ordered therein?

definitions.text: Tries to win many a trial ordered therein?

parts.note: courts means woos or tries to win over
M, the Roman numeral for a thousand, stands for many

indicators.note: ordered means set into a fresh sequence, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone wooing hopes to win, while many trials are ordered there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' rearranges M and A TRIAL into MARTIAL; the whole clue also describes military tribunals where trials are held.
explanation.definitionFit: Military tribunals are where service personnel are tried, many cases being ordered there.

clue.text: Changes in couplet, erasing line as poor verse

indicators.note: changes means the remaining letters are altered into a new order
erasing means rubbing out, so this letter is removed

explanation.surface: Revisions to a couplet strip out a line and leave weak verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'erasing' removes L from IN COUPLET, leaving INCOUPET, which 'Changes' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Bad verse lacks the qualities of real poetry, so it is unlyrical.

clue.text: Discharged again from pipe carrying fuel

indicators.note: carrying means holding within, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a reed is a simple pipe or wind instrument
peat is a fuel cut from bogs

explanation.surface: A gun was fired a second time from a pipe that held fuel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discharged again' suggests a patient, but it means a gun fired once more; 'carrying' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Repeated can mean fired or done once more, as a weapon is discharged again.

clue.text: Streetwise tabloid's pests

parts.note: fly is British slang for sharp or streetwise
a tabloid is a newspaper, a paper

explanation.surface: A savvy tabloid exposes nuisances.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: a sticky sheet is a paper for catching insect pests.
explanation.definitionFit: This sticky strip is meant for trapping flies and similar insect nuisances.

clue.text: Shame about old Left's form of government

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece wraps round the other

parts.note: a shame is a pity, as in what a shame
L is the usual abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: It is a pity about the old Left's style of governing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts O and L inside PITY.
explanation.definitionFit: A polity is an organised state or a type of civil government.

clue.text: Hard-hitting? Weak about Church

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the weak word wraps round the other

parts.note: puny means feeble or weak

explanation.surface: A weak sermon is set against a forceful one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard-hitting?' looks like a description of a boxer; 'about' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Punchy means forceful, delivering a strong impact.

clue.text: Good to intervene in Scots town that's raised minor problem

indicators.note: to intervene is to come between, so this letter goes inside
raised in a down clue means read upwards, that is backwards

parts.note: Elgin is a town in Moray in the north of Scotland

explanation.surface: A good person steps in at a Scottish town where a small problem has come up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns ELGIN into NIGLE in this down clue; 'to intervene in' puts G inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A niggle is a small worry or irritation.

clue.text: Author showing soldiers with expertise

parts.note: OR stands for other ranks, soldiers who are not officers
doing something well means doing it with skill

explanation.surface: A writer displays troops handled skilfully.
explanation.definitionFit: George Orwell wrote Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four.

clue.text: Quick to remove first danger

indicators.note: to remove first means the opening letter is dropped

parts.note: brisk means quick or lively

explanation.surface: Acting fast to get rid of the main hazard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to remove first' drops B from BRISK.
explanation.definitionFit: A risk is a hazard or chance of harm.

clue.text: A red light mostly damaged pupil at the top

indicators.note: damaged means broken up, so the letters are rearranged
mostly means most of the word, with its final letter removed

explanation.surface: A broken red light is spotted on the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' cuts T from LIGHT; 'damaged' rearranges A RED plus LIGH.
explanation.definitionFit: The leading schoolgirl, chosen to represent the student body, is a British school role.

clue.text: Help foolish person, one taking particular position

parts.note: an ass is a fool
one is the Roman numeral I
a stance is a stated position or attitude

explanation.surface: A fool takes a firm stand on something.
explanation.definitionFit: Assistance means aid or support.

clue.text: Look at this attempt to produce a symbol

parts.note: lo is an old exclamation meaning look
a go is a try or attempt

explanation.surface: An attempt at designing an emblem is shown off.
explanation.definitionFit: A logo is an emblem or badge that represents a company.
